summary: All three hypotheses in Iteration 3 were confirmed: the paper's ITL = α/(1−ρ) formula systematically underperforms a simple linear fit across the full rate range (R² 0.92–0.95 vs 0.976–0.985), and its overprediction grows monotonically from <1% at low rates to >50–108% at rate=150 req/s. The formula is accurate only in the low-rate steady-state regime (MAPE <0.08% at rates 5–20 req/s), and its breakdown at high rates is explained by finite-horizon transient effects rather than a fundamental modeling error.
key_points: Formula vs. linear fit (R²): Best-fit 1/(1−ρ) achieves R²=0.919 (AL) and 0.947 (AD) — both below 0.95. Simple linear fit achieves R²=0.976 (AL) and 0.985 (AD) — both above 0.95. Linear wins across the full 5–150 req/s range.

Overprediction is strictly monotone increasing: At rate=20 req/s the formula overpredicts by <0.25% (confirming near-steady-state accuracy); at rate=150 req/s it overpredicts by 108.6% (AL) and 49.9% (AD), far exceeding the predicted thresholds of >50% and >30% respectively.

Root cause confirmed — finite-horizon transient effects: The 300-request simulation never reaches steady-state batch size at high rates, so the positive feedback loop (large batch → slower → larger batch) assumed by the formula never fully engages. The formula is structurally correct but operationally inapplicable for finite-horizon workloads above ~20 req/s.
w_AL > w_AD confirmed (0.004707 vs 0.003685): Consistent with the paper's prediction that aggregated-local mode carries more per-request overhead than disaggregated-decode-only mode.

What's still unknown: Whether increasing request count (e.g., 3000 requests) allows the simulation to reach true steady state and restores formula accuracy at high rates; how variable token lengths affect the fit; and whether a modified saturating formula (e.g., α·(1+c·rate)) better captures finite-horizon behavior.

Recommended next iteration: Run with a much larger request count (e.g., 3000) at high rates to test whether steady-state is reached and the formula recovers accuracy — this would cleanly separate 'formula is wrong' from 'finite-horizon prevents steady-state,' which is the remaining open question.
